title: A simple-root wall changes a Frobenius-kernel highest vector reversibly
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $S$ be a semisimple simply connected affine $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme]. Here semisimple means smooth, connected and of finite type with no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup; solvable means that iterated commutator subgroup schemes eventually become trivial. Simply connected means that every surjective homomorphism from a semisimple group scheme with finite central kernel is an isomorphism, where finite means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra and central means commuting after every scalar extension. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq C\subseteq S$ and a Borel subgroup $C$. A split torus is a product of copies of $\mathbf G_m$, with $\mathbf G_m(D)=D^\times$; maximal means maximal under inclusion, and Borel means maximal smooth connected solvable closed subgroup. Write $U=R_u(C)$ for its largest smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup; unipotent means unipotent geometric matrices in a faithful representation. Use $C=U\rtimes T$, the character lattice $X^*(T)=\operatorname{Hom}(T,\mathbf G_m)$, positive roots $\Psi$ in $\operatorname{Lie}(C)$, their simple-root base $\Delta_C$, and coroots from [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. The pairing is determined by $\mu\circ\alpha^\vee(t)=t^{\langle\mu,\alpha^\vee\rangle}$. Choose $\alpha\in\Delta_C$. Let $n_\alpha\in N_S(T)(F)$ represent the reflection $s_\alpha(\chi)=\chi-\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ of [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections], where $N_S(T)(F)$ consists of the elements conjugating $T$ to itself. Put $C'=n_\alpha Cn_\alpha^{-1}$. Its positive roots are $(\Psi\setminus\{\alpha\})\cup\{-\alpha\}$.

Fix $r\ge1$ and $q=p^r$. For every affine $F$-group $K$, put $K^{(q)}=\operatorname{Spec}(F[K]\otimes_{F,a\mapsto a^q}F)$ and $K_r=\ker(F^r_{K/F}:K\to K^{(q)})$, where the relative Frobenius has coordinate map $c\otimes a\mapsto ac^q$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Assume $S_r$ is finite. For its closed subgroup kernels use $\operatorname{Dist}(K_r)=\operatorname{Hom}_F(F[K_r],F)$, with product $(ab)(f)=(a\otimes b)(\Delta_K f)$ and unit evaluation at the identity [def-sfb-affine-group-distribution-calculus]. Regard their distribution algebras as subalgebras of $A=\operatorname{Dist}(S_r)$ by the duals of coordinate restriction. Choose arbitrary root parametrizations $x_{\pm\alpha}:\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}U_{\pm\alpha}$ [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations], with $\mathbf G_a(D)=(D,+)$, and put $d_{\pm\alpha}^{(j)}(f)=[t^j]x_{\pm\alpha}^*f$ for $0\le j<q$ on the $r$th kernels.

Let $\mu\in X^*(T)$ satisfy the integer equality $\langle\mu,\alpha^\vee\rangle=q-1$. Let $V$ be any left unital $A$-module, meaning an $F$-vector space with a unital $F$-algebra map $A\to\operatorname{End}_F(V)$, and $w\in V$. Extend a character of $T$ to a Borel containing $T$ by composing with its projection onto $T$ along its unipotent radical. Write $\widetilde\mu_C$ for this extension of $\mu$ to $C$. Suppose
$$b\cdot w=b(\widetilde\mu_C|_{C_r})w\qquad(b\in\operatorname{Dist}(C_r)).$$
Set $\mu'=\mu-(q-1)\alpha$ and $w'=d_{-\alpha}^{(q-1)}w$, and let $\widetilde{\mu'}_{C'}$ be the extension of $\mu'$ to $C'$. One has
$$b'\cdot w'=b'(\widetilde{\mu'}_{C'}|_{C'_r})w'\qquad(b'\in\operatorname{Dist}(C'_r)),$$
and there is $\kappa\in F^\times$ such that
$$d_\alpha^{(q-1)}w'=\kappa w.$$
In particular $w\ne0$ implies $w'\ne0$. No rational $S$-action on $V$ and no lower bound on $p$ are assumed; the assertion includes $p=2$ and every $r\ge1$.

source.place: Agent-formulated finite-kernel adjacent-Borel lemma. Geometric inputs: review of SL2, 20.37--20.41, printed pp.422--423; rank-one homomorphism and reflection, Theorem 21.11, printed pp.428--430; root bases, C.21--C.22, printed p.612. Milne does not state this finite-kernel module lemma. WANTED: Jantzen, Representations of Algebraic Groups (2003), II.3.18 and II.9, for the infinitesimal intertwining calculation.

proof.text: Put $m=q-1$. We may use points of the finite group scheme $S_r$ on $V$ without assuming a rational $S$-action. Indeed, choose an $F$-basis $(c_i)$ of $F[S_r]$ and its dual basis $(a_i)$ in $A$. Define $\rho(v)=\sum_i(a_i v)\otimes c_i$. Evaluating the two coassociativity expressions against $a\otimes b$ gives respectively $(ab)v$ and $a(bv)$; evaluating the counit gives $1_Av=v$. Thus this is a coaction, independent of the basis, and gives an action of $S_r(D)$ on $V\otimes_F D$ for every commutative $F$-algebra $D$. For a closed subgroup $K\subseteq S_r$, the equality $bv=b(\chi)v$ for all $b\in F[K]^*$ is equivalent, by dual-basis evaluation, to $\rho_K(v)=v\otimes\chi$, hence to $kv=\chi(k)v$ on every test algebra. In particular the hypothesis makes $w$ fixed by $U_r$ and a $T_r$-eigenvector of character $\mu$.

source.place: Chapter 10, distributions and coordinate coactions; agent finite-dimensional dual-basis calculation, using the convolution and coaction definitions in def-sfb-affine-group-distribution-calculus.

proof.text: Choose the homomorphism $v_\alpha:\operatorname{SL}_2\to S$ of the cited opposite-root parametrization node. Write $y_\pm(t)=v_\alpha(I_2+tE_{12/21})$ and $h(z)=\alpha^\vee(z)$. These give compatible coordinates on $U_{\pm\alpha}$ and satisfy $v_\alpha(\operatorname{diag}(z,z^{-1}))=h(z)$. The given coordinates have the form $x_\pm(t)=y_\pm(a_\pm t)$ for $a_\pm\in F^\times$: composing two isomorphisms with $\mathbf G_a$ gives a polynomial automorphism of the affine line with polynomial inverse, so its degree is one, and its constant term is zero. Set $E_j(f)=[t^j]y_+^*f$ and $F_j(f)=[t^j]y_-^*f$, $0\le j<q$. Then $d_{\alpha}^{(j)}=a_+^jE_j$ and $d_{-\alpha}^{(j)}=a_-^jF_j$. Every group homomorphism commutes with relative Frobenius: on coordinate rings this is just $f^*(c^q)=f^*(c)^q$. Thus $v_\alpha$ restricts to $\operatorname{SL}_{2,r}\to S_r$, so all subsequent truncated matrix calculations act on the module of step 1.

source.place: Theorem 21.11(b)--(e), printed pp.429--430, and 21.24, p.432; agent coordinate rescaling and Frobenius naturality.

proof.text: Apply the standard-parabolic Levi statement with $I=\{\alpha\}$. Its Levi $L$ has roots $\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$, and $P=R\rtimes L$, $C=R\rtimes C_L$, where $R$ is normal in $P$ and $C_L=C\cap L$. The rank-one reflection statement gives a representative in $L$ of $s_\alpha$. Any chosen $n_\alpha$ differs from this representative by an element of $T(F)$; hence $n_\alpha\in L(F)$ and it normalizes $R$. The Borel-pair statement and the root-product coordinates applied to the reductive group $L$ give $C_L=U_\alpha\rtimes T$; there is only one positive root. Its conjugate has the single positive root $-\alpha$, so $n_\alpha C_Ln_\alpha^{-1}=U_{-\alpha}\rtimes T$, by the same two statements. Consequently $C'=R\rtimes(U_{-\alpha}\rtimes T)$. These are identities of group schemes, not just of their $F$-points. They restrict to Frobenius kernels: Frobenius commutes with multiplication, and under each product isomorphism its kernel is the product of the kernels of the factors. In particular $C'_r$ has underlying scheme $R_r\times U_{-\alpha,r}\times T_r$. Conjugation by $n_\alpha$ carries the $\beta$-weight space of $\operatorname{Lie}(C)$ to the $s_\alpha\beta$-weight space, so the positive roots of $C'$ are $s_\alpha(\Psi)$. Here $s_\alpha\alpha=-\alpha$; a root $\beta\in\Psi\setminus\{\alpha\}$ is not a multiple of $\alpha$, since $\mathbf Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\pm\alpha\}$ by the rank-one reflection statement, so it has a positive coefficient at a simple root other than $\alpha$. The root $s_\alpha\beta=\beta-\langle\beta,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ keeps that coefficient, hence is positive by the same-sign property of the Borel-pair statement. As $s_\alpha$ is injective, $s_\alpha(\Psi)=(\Psi\setminus\{\alpha\})\cup\{-\alpha\}$, as asserted in the statement.

source.place: Proposition 21.90 and Theorem 21.91, printed pp.453--454 (Levi and radical); Theorem 21.11(d), p.429 (reflection in the rank-one centralizer); Theorem 21.68(a),(b), p.445 (Borel product).

proof.text: Let $v_0=F_mw$, so $w'=a_-^m v_0$. Since $R\subseteq U$, step 1 says $w$ is fixed by $R_r$. Normality of $R$ in $P$ implies that $U_{-\alpha,r}$ normalizes $R_r$ (conjugation commutes with Frobenius). For any test algebra $D$, $g\in U_{-\alpha,r}(D)$ and $z\in R_r(D)$, one has $z(gw)=g((g^{-1}zg)w)=gw$. Use the universal point $g=y_-(t)$ over $F[t]/(t^q)$, and compare the coefficient of $t^m$. This gives $zv_0=v_0$ after every scalar extension: coefficients are compared over $D[t]/(t^q)$. Thus $R_r$ fixes $v_0$ and $w'$. This explicitly supplies the invariant-subspace argument for finite kernels.

source.place: Theorem 21.91, printed pp.453--454, normality in the Levi semidirect product; agent three-factor conjugation identity and coefficient extraction.

proof.text: For any test algebra $D$ and $z\in T_r(D)$ the root conjugation formula gives $z y_-(t)z^{-1}=y_-(\alpha(z)^{-1}t)$. Apply this identity to $w$, use $zw=\mu(z)w$, and compare coefficients in $D[t]/(t^q)$. It yields $zv_0=\mu(z)\alpha(z)^{-m}v_0=\mu'(z)v_0$, and the same holds for $w'$. This uses the full characters on $T_r$, including its nonreduced points, rather than differentials of weights.

source.place: 21.19, formula (135), printed p.431; agent coefficient extraction in the negative-root coordinate.

proof.text: The additive-group identity $y_-(s)y_-(t)=y_-(s+t)$ can be evaluated over $F[s,t]/(s^q,t^q)$, since $(s+t)^q=s^q+t^q=0$. By the definition of $F_j$, its action on $w$ is $\sum_{j=0}^{m}(s+t)^j F_jw$. The coefficient of $t^m$ is exactly $F_mw$ and has no $s$-dependence: terms with $j<m$ have too small degree and there is no term with $j>m$. On the left the same coefficient is $y_-(s)v_0$. Therefore $U_{-\alpha,r}$ fixes $v_0$ and $w'$.

source.place: Chapter 10, coordinate coactions; agent calculation in the coordinate algebra of the additive Frobenius kernel, using the root coordinates of step 2.

proof.text: By the product isomorphism in step 3, every $D$-point of $C'_r$, for every $F$-algebra $D$, has the form $z_-ut$ with $z_-\in R_r(D)$, $u\in U_{-\alpha,r}(D)$ and $t\in T_r(D)$. Steps 4--6 give $(z_-ut)w'=\mu'(t)w'$. This is the extended character $\widetilde{\mu'}_{C'}$ evaluated on this point: $R_u(C')=n_\alpha Un_\alpha^{-1}$ contains $R=n_\alpha Rn_\alpha^{-1}$ and $U_{-\alpha}=n_\alpha U_\alpha n_\alpha^{-1}$ (step 3), so the projection $C'=R_u(C')\rtimes T\to T$ of the Borel-pair statement sends $z_-ut$ to $t$. Equivalently, evaluating at the universal point in $D=F[C'_r]$ gives $\rho_{C'_r}(w')=w'\otimes\widetilde{\mu'}_{C'}$. Apply any $b'\in F[C'_r]^*$ to the second factor to obtain the required distribution eigenvector equality.

source.place: Chapter 10, coordinate coactions; agent application of the finite duality of step 1 to the group-scheme product from step 3.

proof.text:
For recovery work over $D=F[u,v]/(u^q,v^q)$ and put $a=1+uv$. The element $a$ is a unit and $a^q=1$. Direct multiplication of determinant-one $2\times2$ matrices gives, in the compatible coordinates of step 2,
$$y_+(u)y_-(v)=y_-(v/a)h(a)y_+(u/a).$$
All factors lie in the corresponding $r$th Frobenius kernels: $(u/a)^q=(v/a)^q=0$ and $a^q=1$. Since $U_{\alpha,r}$ fixes $w$ and $h(a)w=a^{\langle\mu,\alpha^\vee\rangle}w=a^m w$, applying the identity to $w$ gives
$$\sum_{i,j=0}^{m}u^iv^j E_iF_jw=\sum_{j=0}^{m}v^j(1+uv)^{m-j}F_jw.$$
The coefficient of $u^mv^m$ on the left is $E_mF_mw$. On the right a term with $j>0$ has $u$-degree at most $m-j<m$; the $j=0$ term contributes $[u^mv^m](1+uv)^m w=w$. Hence $E_mF_mw=w$. This is a polynomial calculation with integer coefficients reduced to $F$; it divides by no factorial and uses no assertion about global $S$-modules.

source.place: Review of SL2, 20.37--20.41, printed pp.422--423, and Theorem 21.11, pp.429--430; agent explicit Gauss matrix multiplication and coefficient calculation.

proof.text:
Finally step 2 and $E_mF_mw=w$ imply
$$d_\alpha^{(m)}w'=a_+^ma_-^m E_mF_mw=(a_+a_-)^m w.$$
Take $\kappa=(a_+a_-)^m\in F^\times$. If $w'=0$, the displayed equality forces $w=0$. This also covers $w=0$ without choosing a scalar depending on $w$.

source.place: Agent scalar substitution following the compatible root coordinates and the explicit coefficient calculation.
